items.name: Day 1 · First 24 hours after a crash
items.hook: Crashes happen on I-275 and I-4 every day — what you do in the first 24 hours quietly decides what your claim is worth.

script.line: Crashes happen on I-275 and I-4 every day. The first 24 hours quietly decide what your claim is worth.
Most people lose value here without realizing it. Three things protect you.
One: see a doctor today, even if you feel fine. Adrenaline hides injuries.
Two: photograph everything — cars, scene, injuries, the other plate.
Three: hold off on a recorded statement to their insurer until you've talked to someone.
Save this so you have it if you ever need it, and follow for the rest.

items.caption: The first day matters more than people think. Save it in case you're ever in a wreck around Tampa. Free review in bio.

items.hook: The first check the insurer offers after a crash is rarely the real number — here's what to know before you sign.

script.line: The first check the insurer offers after a crash is rarely the real number.
It usually lands before anyone knows the full cost of an injury.
And once you sign, it's final. You can't reopen it.
So bills that show up later come out of your pocket, not theirs.
Before you accept anything, have it read by someone who does this daily.

items.name: Day 4 · 5 mistakes that quietly hurt your claim
items.hook: 5 mistakes that quietly hurt a Florida injury claim

slides.heading: 5 mistakes that quietly hurt your injury claim
slides.body: Most people make at least two in the first week. Swipe.

slides.heading: 1. Waiting to get treated
slides.body: A gap between the crash and your first visit becomes the main argument that you weren't really hurt.

slides.heading: 2. Posting about it
slides.body: An 'I'm okay, just shaken!' post gets screenshotted and used later. Go quiet for now.

slides.heading: 3. Rushing into a recorded statement
slides.body: You're usually not required to give one right away — vague answers get used to shrink a claim.

slides.heading: 4. Taking the first offer
slides.body: Usually a starting point, not a fair number. Once you sign, the case is closed.

slides.heading: 5. Handling the adjuster solo
slides.body: They negotiate these daily; you're doing it once, while injured. Even the table first.

items.name: Day 6 · How we build a truck-accident case
items.hook: Here's how we actually build a truck-accident case — no dollar promises, just the work.

script.line: Here's how we actually build a truck-accident case. No promises — just the work.
On freight corridors like I-4, truck data and dashcam footage can be overwritten in days.
So a preservation letter goes out immediately, before anything's gone.
Then we find everyone responsible — driver, carrier, even the maintenance shop.
And we prepare like it's going to trial, because that's when cases resolve well.

items.name: Day 11 · The 3 photos to take at the scene
items.hook: If you're ever in a crash, take these 3 photos before you leave the scene.

script.line: If you're ever in a crash, take these 3 photos before you leave.
One: the wide shot — both cars, where they ended up, the whole scene.
Two: the close-ups — damage on both cars, and any injuries you can see.
Three: the details — the other plate, their insurance card, the street signs.
Scenes get cleared in minutes. These photos can't be re-created later.

items.name: Day 15 · The one thing not to say to the adjuster
items.hook: When the adjuster calls after your crash, there's one thing you should never say.

script.line: When the adjuster calls, there's one thing you should never say.
It's the reflex answer: 'I'm fine.'
You're being polite — but injuries can take days to show, and that line gets quoted back.
Instead: 'I'm still being evaluated, I'll follow up in writing.'
You're not lying — you're just not guessing about your own health on the spot.

items.caption: 'I'm fine' is the most expensive thing people say after a crash. Here's the better line. Save it.

items.name: Day 22 · A gap in treatment can shrink your claim
items.hook: Skipping appointments after a crash quietly shrinks your claim — even if you're tough.

script.line: Skipping appointments after a crash quietly shrinks your claim.
Here's why: a gap in treatment becomes 'see, they got better.'
Even if you were just busy or toughing it out, it reads the same on paper.
If your provider says keep coming, keep coming — for your body and your case.
Consistency is the cheapest thing that protects you.

items.hook: If the crash report got the fault wrong, that is not the end of your case.

script.line: If the crash report got fault wrong, that's not the end of your case.
A report is one officer's snapshot — it isn't a verdict.
Witnesses, camera footage, and the physical damage can tell a different story.
So if it feels wrong, don't give up — get it looked at before you accept blame.
